Working Session Recap

Last week, in collaboration with AUDA NEPAD, we hosted a working session in Stellenbosch for our project launched earlier this year titled “Africa’s Development Agenda for its Green Minerals”.

This project has brought together scholars to craft policy papers and briefs to analyze African governments' plans for mineral-driven industrialization and manufacturing. This included in-depth country case studies, exploring ambitious mineral strategies and their essential requirements, such as the DRC-Zambia battery industry MoU, South Africa's PGM endeavors, and Zimbabwe's lithium-powered ambitions.

The working session was a platform to discuss the findings and progress of the papers and chart the course for the next phase of the project.
A special acknowledgment to Mkhululi N Ncube from African Minerals Development  Centre  (AMDC) and Melaku Desta of Africa Trade Policy Centre at UNECA for their invaluable contributions as discussion facilitators.

Our gratitude goes out to Pamla Gopaul, Axel Rusenga, and Dr. Mustafa Sakr of AUDA NEPAD for pleasantly hosting us. We especially thank Saliem Fakir of The African Climate Foundation and Fred Kabanda of African Development Bank Group for their valuable presence.

A big thank you to our project leads, Dr. Olumide Abimbola, Patience, Amir Lebdioui, and all the contributors who have dedicated their expertise to this project.

We will continue to use this space to share project updates in due course!

Very happy to see this published! Proposing a 'DEEP' approach to AI: 

🇩 Democratise and demystify, and make it understandable to all
🇪 Empower people to use AI to improve their lives and livelihoods
🇪 Explore and experiment with AI, safely and securely
🇵 Protect people from the negative impacts of AI.

And AI is a truly global discussion and exploration. AI is more than Silicon Valley. It’s about the Silicon Savannah in Kenya, where AI startups are approaching $100m in funding. It’s about an emerging regional approach from Latin America, Thailand’s efforts to shape an AI ecosystem by 2027, and everywhere in between. Many of the exciting, important, and cutting-edge explorations of AI are being undertaken in ‘developing’ countries. 🌍 Inspired by the Youth4Climate: #SparkingSolutions Event
 
Last week, I had the privilege of being part of the selection panel for the Energy thematic at the Youth4Climate: Sparking Solutions event in Rome. Witnessing the passion, dedication, and innovative spirit of the youth presenting their energy projects was truly remarkable.
 
Gathering from 63 countries, these young minds came together with a 100 youth-driven solutions, all with a shared goal of creating a meaningful impact on our planet. The level of creativity and thoughtfulness in their projects was truly impressive.
 
At the event, I had the honor of witnessing some incredible project pitches from the youth. These innovative solutions included ideas such as harnessing affordable and renewable heating sources like Biomass, a high-performing stove that can save up to 5 tons of CO2 emissions, and initiatives to promote the use of solar power in off-grid schools and community centres. These ideas are not only impressive but also represent tangible steps towards reducing our carbon footprint and promoting #cleanenergy solutions. It's a testament to their dedication and ingenuity.
 
Taking part in the #Youth4Climate event reaffirmed my conviction: the future of our planet is in the hands of the next generation, and they are ready to take on the challenge. But we need to empower them, provide the support they need, and enable them to implement  their ideas so that #sustainableenergy use becomes the norm, not the exception.
 
The #Youth4Climate initiative, co-led by the UNDP Rome Centre  and Ministero dell'Ambiente e della Sicurezza Energetica  funding, mentorship programs, and capacity-building opportunities, these young climate leaders will have the tools to turn their innovative ideas into reality.

#EnergyForDevelopment

My new  book, “Revisiting the Ocean: Living the Blue Economy” builds on the foundation laid in my previous work, “Rethinking the Oceans”. In this sequel, I reinforce the idea that the Ocean is a valuable ecosystem that can drive sustainable economic growth while ensuring its health and protection.
It is no secret that the greater part
our planet is the sea. Yet we continue to treat it as less important than land. The Ocean is our greatest hope for the future. It is time we see it for what it is. My book urges us to do just that. I realise the challenges we face as well as to the multitude of wonderful initiatives. Whether we focus on new sources of renewable energy, or the work of volunteers restoring our beaches and protecting wildlife; whether it is the immense contribution that can be made by the inventive use of seaweed, or business startups for which nothing is impossible - all mark a turning of the tide. We should take heed. If we are willing to put our trust in the Ocean, we can yet win the day. 
My new book -“Revisiting the Ocean - Living the Blue Economy” is a book of hope !

Last month, a BIG news came out of the palm oil industry, with significant (positive) implications for the wider agri-commodities sector!

The Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil (RSPO) announced the appointment of a tripartite consortium comprising of leading agritech firms Agridence , CIED , and NGIS “to develop a unified, bespoke Certification, Trade, and Traceability System (CTTS)”.

The keyword here – at least for me – is ‘traceability’, which has been a longstanding challenge for the industry. This is because of complex supply chains and difficulties in tracking palm oil from small-scale producers, who make up a large part of the commodity production.

RSPO’s revamped digital system would essentially aim to streamline and integrate RSPO’s sustainable palm oil certification, audit, and risk assessment processes into a secure trading platform, enabling end-to-end traceability of palm oil.

This comes as a major relief to palm oil corporates, who are under pressure from the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR), which will come into effect from December 2024. EUDR mandates that importers of deforestation-risk commodities (e.g., palm oil, cocoa, timber, natural rubber) and their derived products into the EU market must be able to prove that the products do not originate from recently deforested or degraded land.

The new system to be developed by the consortium, led by Singapore-based Agridence, could be instrumental for demonstrating the sustainable origin of RSPO-certified palm oil, especially from major producers Indonesia and Malaysia. The system will leverage Agridence’s experience and expertise from building a similar platform for the natural rubber industry.

At Singapore Agri-Food Innovation Lab (SAIL) , we are engaged in exploring innovations, learnings, and best practices from different industries and supporting their adaptation and adoption by our Corporate Partners and stakeholders to drive sustainability in the wider agri-food sector.

History was made on the first day of the UN Climate Conference, #COP28 . UNDP Maldives welcomes the historic agreement to operationalize the Loss and Damage Fund and funding arrangements and acknowledges the unwavering efforts made by Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS) and the Maldivian Government with its members of the transitional committee who worked tirelessly to get us to this point.

In conjunction with this momentous development, we are delighted to present a new paper titled 'Loss and Damage and Climate Litigation: How Can the Maldives and other Small Island Developing States (SIDS) Position Itself for Greater Climate Action.' Authored by UNDP Maldives in collaboration with Frankfurt School of Finance & Management , the paper advocates for a unified climate governance strategy, empowering vulnerable SIDS like the Maldives with reforms and strategic options to embrace this innovative instrument of climate justice now in action.

The paper explores the critical nexus between climate-related loss and damage and the recent surge in climate litigation. It argues that SIDS should lead robust and equitable climate action, navigating the complex relationship between climate change, human rights, and legal responsibilities. The paper advocates for enhanced funding for SIDS, rooted in the principles of loss and damage, utilizing both traditional and novel financing mechanisms.

The recommendations within the paper urge #SIDS to spearhead climate resilience initiatives, employing innovative financial and insurance strategies. It underscores the need for exhaustive data collection and risk assessments to strengthen early warning systems and devise disaster risk strategies. To effectively manage and foresee climate litigation risks, it calls for educational initiatives on climate liability, incentivization of private sector adaptation, and harmonization of national legal frameworks with environmental pledges.

The overarching aim is to develop a cohesive approach that integrates financial risk management, climate adaptation, and active engagement in the development of international climate finance mechanisms. While primarily intended for the Maldives, the insights also hold relevance for other nations.

My New Book “Revisiting the Ocean - Living the Blue Economy”
It is a book of Hope. It looks to the future based on the growing number of ordinary people, NGOs, philanthropists, startup enthusiasts, scientists throughout the world trying to find solutions to resolve the pressing problems of the Ocean and Planet. In my book I look at the Ocean, being the last frontier - the Blue Economy and what it means for the future of the human race.

The Blue Economy is synonymous with the safe and sustainable use of the ocean. It replaces years of neglect and wilful harm with a respect for beauty and combined with utility; a resource to be shared fairly by all humanity; an enduring habitat for marine life in its entirety; a source of enjoyment and fulfillment; the assertion of spiritual values in harmony with material needs. It will be a credit to all who inhabit this planet, the ultimate triumph of the benign and creative side of human nature. The ocean holds the key to our very survival; The Ocean is our future.
